**Mathematical Formulation**

Let:

---

A distribution is an ordered triple \((a,b,c) \in \mathbb{N}_0^3\) satisfying:

1. **Sum condition:** \( a + b + c = 30 \).
2. **At-least-2 condition:** \( \max(a,b,c) \ge 2 \) (automatically true due to sum, but included for completeness).
3. **Difference condition:** There exist indices \( i \neq j \) such that \( |a_i - a_j| = 6 \).

Let  
\[
S_{\text{ordered}} = \left\{ (a,b,c) \in \mathbb{N}_0^3 \; \middle| \; a+b+c=30,\; \max(a,b,c) \ge 2,\; \exists i\neq j: |a_i - a_j| = 6 \right\}.
\]

Because the boxes are indistinguishable after shuffling, the adversary’s choice is effectively a multiset of three numbers. We can therefore work with nondecreasing triples. Define  
\[
T = \left\{ (a,b,c) \in \mathbb{N}_0^3 \; \middle| \; a \le b \le c,\; a+b+c=30,\; (b-a=6 \text{ or } c-b=6 \text{ or } c-a=6) \right\}.
\]
Every valid distribution is a permutation of some element of \(T\).

---

### 2. Bob’s strategy  
Bob chooses an ordered triple of guesses \( g = (g_1, g_2, g_3) \in \mathbb{N}_0^3 \), one for each box. Since the boxes are indistinguishable, we may assume without loss of optimality that guesses are in nondecreasing order. Moreover, guesses larger than 30 are never beneficial (any actual number is at most 30). Thus, we restrict to  
\[
G = \left\{ (g_1,g_2,g_3) \in \mathbb{N}_0^3 \; \middle| \; 0 \le g_1 \le g_2 \le g_3 \le 30 \right\}.
\]

\[
w_\pi(g,a) = \sum_{i=1}^3 \begin{cases} g_i & \text{if } g_i \le a_{\pi(i)}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}
\]  
The adversary chooses the permutation that minimizes Bob’s winnings:

\[

The optimal strategy \(g^*\) is any \(g \in G\) attaining this maximum.
